title: Intolerance

evidence.note: Published in the US on September 5, 1916. US works published in 1930 or earlier have completed their 95-year term (Duke CSPD: works from 1930 entered the public domain on January 1, 2026). A 1916 work is well past that, so the film print is public domain by term expiry.
evidence.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain, Public Domain Day 2026

evidence.note: The original 1916 score credits are Joseph Carl Breil and Julián Carrillo, and that music is also old enough to be free. The silent images are free, but modern copies usually carry a newer score. Carl Davis composed a score for the 1989 Thames Silents/Photoplay restoration, and Joseph Turrin wrote a synthetic orchestral score for the 2002 Kino International release. Those recordings and compositions are separate works with their own protection.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Intolerance (film), used as a secondary summary only

evidence.note: The screenplay is an original work by Griffith, written in response to criticism of The Birth of a Nation. It is not adapted from a source with a later term, so the story layer follows the film's own status.
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Intolerance (film), used as a secondary summary only

evidence.note: Several modern restorations exist: the 1989 Thames Silents/Photoplay version (Kevin Brownlow and David Gill) with restored tints and a Carl Davis score, a 1989 Gillian Anderson, MoMA and Library of Congress version, and a 2002 Kino International release with a Joseph Turrin score. A faithful restoration of a public-domain print adds no new US copyright. Added scores, new titles and other new material can be protected.

editorial:
Intolerance is D. W. Griffith's 1916 silent epic. It interweaves four stories: Babylon, Judea, Renaissance France and modern America. The film was released in the US on September 5, 1916, and Griffith made it as a response to the criticism of his earlier film The Birth of a Nation. A creator can use the footage freely: the print's US copyright term has run out, and the 1916 score by Joseph Carl Breil and Julián Carrillo is also old enough to be free.

The trap is the version you copy. The 1989 Photoplay/Thames Silents restoration carries a Carl Davis orchestral score, and the 2002 Kino release carries a Joseph Turrin score. Those scores and recordings are protected separately, as is any new material added in a restoration. Take the images from a source with no modern score, or commission or license new music. The trademark layer has not been checked.
faq: Can I reuse footage from the Kino or Photoplay releases of Intolerance?

The 1916 images are free in the US. The Carl Davis score on the Photoplay/Thames version and the Joseph Turrin score on the Kino release are separately protected, as may be any added titles or other new material. A faithful restoration of the picture adds no copyright to it. Use the picture without the soundtrack, or use an unscored copy such as an archive transfer.
Does the story of Intolerance carry any separate rights?

No. Griffith wrote the screenplay himself and it was not adapted from a later-protected source, so it follows the film's own status. The trademark layer is undetermined, because no active mark has been checked.
